speaker_role: former admissions reader/interviewer (NYU, including scholarship program interviews); now an independent counselor at InGenius Prep
commercial_incentive: channel promotes a free admissions consultation link; speaker currently works as a paid InGenius Prep counselor
key_insights: NYU looks for applicants who take risks, embrace diversity, and are genuinely curious about being immersed in an unconventional, non-campus, city-integrated college experience.

NYU's international campuses (Shanghai, Abu Dhabi) function as full home campuses rather than study-abroad semesters, so students should only rank locations they'd genuinely attend since transferring between them afterward is difficult.

NYU's early decision rounds give an admissions edge but come with historically less generous financial aid, so ED1 is recommended mainly for students certain of NYU who can accept whatever aid is offered; ED2 suits students rejected elsewhere.
Because NYU has flexible/test-optional policies, students can submit AP, IB, or subject-test scores instead of SAT/ACT to demonstrate strength in specific subjects when overall test scores are weak.
Application review sorts students into rough categories (likely admit, borderline, likely deny) after assessing transcript rigor first, then activities, recommendations, and essays.
The most common mistake in NYU's supplemental 'why NYU' essay is centering it on loving New York City rather than NYU's specific programs, research opportunities, or professors.
NYU tracks demonstrated interest, including routine social media engagement, campus tours, and direct contact with admissions officers.
Personal statements that simply restate the activities list waste an opportunity; the strongest essays reveal personality, humor, and an authentic personal voice instead.
specific_numbers_or_facts: NYU's 'Why NYU' supplemental essay is capped at 400 words, per Lydia Mason
NYU accepts SAT/ACT, an IB diploma, three SAT subject tests, three AP exam scores, or three IB higher-level exam/A-level results in place of standard testing, per Mason
notable_or_distinctive: Explains NYU's flexible-testing menu (subject tests/AP/IB substituting for SAT/ACT) and the practical downside of NYU's multiple global campuses being hard to transfer between, details not commonly covered elsewhere.
reliability_notes: Speaker's admissions-reader experience predates the interview by some years and testing/financial-aid policies likely changed since (interview references the pandemic as recent); the channel's free-consultation offer signals a promotional framing, though the content itself is presented as personal recollection rather than a direct sales pitch.
